title: Seeing gods; the wounded lion
intro: Athena gives Diomedes exceptional sight but also an explicit limit: he may attack Aphrodite, not the other gods. The ensuing lion simile transforms the arrow wound into a source of increased violence. Distinguish what the goddess authorizes from what the hero may later attempt.

notes.text: ἀχλύς is a mist or dimness; ἀχλύν is accusative. ἕλον is first singular unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, ‘I removed,’ not third plural here. ἐπῆεν is an epic imperfect of ἔπειμι, ‘was upon.’ ὄφρα with γιγνώσκῃς gives the purpose: to discriminate gods from men. ἠμέν … ἠδέ means ‘both … and.’

τώ is inferential ‘therefore,’ not a dual pronoun here. αἴ κε equals εἰ ἄν and introduces an eventual condition with subjunctive ἵκηται, aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι, ‘arrive.’ πειρώμενος means ‘making trial [of you].’ μάχεσθαι is an infinitive used as a command, negated by μή; τοῖς ἄλλοις clarifies the prohibited gods.

ἔλθῃσι is third singular second-aorist active subjunctive of ἔρχομαι, with epic -σι added to -ῃ. οὐτάμεν is an epic infinitive in -μεν of οὐτάω, ‘wound,’ used imperativally: ‘wound her!’ τήν emphasizes Aphrodite as the exception. ὀξέϊ is uncontracted dative singular of ὀξύς, agreeing with instrumental χαλκῷ.

ἀπέβη is root-aorist of ἀποβαίνω, ‘departed.’ ἐμίχθη is aorist passive of μίγνυμι, intransitive ‘mingled,’ with dative προμάχοισιν, the front-line fighters. μεμαώς is perfect active participle of μέμονα, ‘be eager,’ with present force. καὶ πρίν περ makes his previous eagerness concessive: keen already, he becomes keener still.

τρὶς τόσσον means ‘three times as much.’ μένος is the subject of ἕλεν, ‘fury seized him.’ The lion is the comparison object: ‘as [fury seizes] a lion.’ The repeated τε throughout the simile marks a typical, recurrent situation, unlike the unique events of the battle narrative.

εἰροπόκος is ‘wool-fleeced’; ὀΐεσσι is epic dative plural of ὄϊς, ‘sheep.’ ὑπεράλμενον is aorist middle participle of ὑπεράλλομαι, ‘leap over,’ with genitive αὐλῆς, the enclosure. χραύσῃ, aorist subjunctive of χραύω, means ‘graze, wound slightly.’ The herdsman hits the lion but does not subdue it.

σθένος is the lion’s force or strength; the herdsman has roused it. προσαμύνει means ‘comes to the defence,’ here of the flock. He instead δύεται, ‘slips / retreats,’ into the σταθμοί, farm buildings or pens. τὰ δ᾽ ἐρῆμα shifts to the abandoned animals: the neuter plural takes singular φοβεῖται, ‘are driven in panic.’

ἀγχιστῖναι means ‘close together,’ feminine plural referring to the sheep. κέχυνται is perfect middle/passive of χέω, literally ‘have been poured,’ vividly ‘are heaped upon one another.’ ἐμμεμαώς intensifies the lion’s eagerness; μίγη is unaugmented second-aorist passive of μίγνυμι, ‘mingled.’ This repeats the human action of ἐμίχθη after the intervening simile.

The two victims are distributed between spear and sword. βαλών is second-aorist participle of βάλλω; πλῆξε is aorist of πλήσσω, ‘struck.’ χαλκήρεϊ means ‘fitted with bronze,’ dative singular with δουρί. κληΐς is the collarbone; κληῖδα is accusative, locating the sword blow by the shoulder.

ἐέργαθεν is a past form of ἐέργω, ‘separate, keep apart’; with ἀπό it describes severing shoulder from neck and back. μετῴχετο is imperfect of μετοίχομαι, ‘went after,’ governing the next victims. τοὺς μὲν ἔασε means he left the previous pair behind: ἔασε is aorist of ἐάω.

ὀνειροπόλος is an interpreter of dreams, here genitive singular in -οιο describing the elderly Eurydamas. ἐκρίνατο is aorist middle of κρίνω, ‘interpret, decide.’ The negative comments bitterly on the inadequacy of his art for these departing sons. ἐρχομένοις is present participle, ‘as they went’; the outcome that explains the remark follows on the next page.
